claim: Tuberculosis caused illness in ten million people in 2019, with 1.4 million deaths.
source: Tuberculosis (TB) is a treatable (primarily) respiratory disease that caused illness in ten million people in 2019, with 1.4million deaths (World Health Organization, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites the World Health Organization, 2020 as the source for the statistics on TB illness and deaths.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 killed more people than TB in 2020 and is likely to do so again in 2021.
source: Ordinarily this is more than any other single pathogen, although SARS-CoV-2 killed more people than TB in 2020 and is likely to do so again in 2021.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and represents an inference about 2021 based on 2020 data.

claim: An increasing proportion of TB cases are resistant to one or more drugs.
source: Like most bacterial diseases treated with antibiotics, an increasing proportion of TB cases are resistant to one or more drugs.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about antibiotic resistance trends in TB.

claim: Tackling antimicrobial resistance will require action on several fronts, including the development of new antibiotics, better stewardship of existing antibiotics and much wider use of antibiotic susceptibility testing.
source: Tackling this 'silent pandemic' will require action on several fronts, including the development of new antibiotics, better stewardship of existing antibiotics and much wider use of antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) to guide prescribing decisions (O'Neill, 2016).
evidence: The claim cites O'Neill, 2016 as the source for the multi-faceted approach to tackling antimicrobial resistance.

claim: M. tuberculosis has an unusually slow doubling time resulting in culture times being weeks rather than days.
source: Compared to most pathogenic bacteria, M. tuberculosis is unusually difficult,mainly because its doubling time is so slow resulting in culture times being weeks rather than days.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about M. tuberculosis growth characteristics.

claim: Most antibiotic prescribing decisions are still done without any AST data.
source: This model, whilst effective, is practically and economically difficult to scale up which explains in part why most antibiotic prescribing decisions are still done without any AST data.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference based on the practical and economic difficulties of scaling up AST.

claim: The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of an antibiotic is the lowest concentration that prevents growth of the pathogen.
source: The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of an antibiotic is the lowest concentration that prevents growth of the pathogen.
evidence: The claim is a standard definition in microbiology.

claim: The accuracy of culture-based AST decreases when the expected MIC is of the same order as the critical concentration.
source: Although simple, the accuracy of such an approach decreases when the expected MIC is of the same order as the critical concentration, as is the case for many antituberculars (CRyPTIC Consortium, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites CRyPTIC Consortium, 2022 as the source for the observation about accuracy limitations.

claim: A crowd of volunteers with no microbiological training can reproducibly and accurately determine the growth of M. tuberculosis on a 96-well plate and the MICs for 13 different antibiotics.
source: In this paper, we shall show that a crowd of volunteers, who have no microbiological training, can reproducibly and accurately determine the growth of M. tuberculosis (the causative agent of TB) on a 96-well plate and thence the MICs for 13 different antibiotics.
evidence: The claim is the main finding of the study and is supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The wisdom of crowds can be traced back to observations made by Galton, 1907.
source: This is an application of the "wisdom of crowds" which can be traced back to observations made by Galton, 1907.
evidence: The claim cites Galton, 1907 as the historical source for the concept of wisdom of crowds.

claim: The Germanic definition of the foot as one sixteenth the combined length of the left feet of the first sixteen men to leave a church on a Sunday is an early use of the wisdom of crowds.
source: An even earlier use is the Germanic definition of the foot as one sixteenth the combined length of the left feet of the first sixteen men to leave a church on a Sunday (Koebel, 1563).
evidence: The claim cites Koebel, 1563 as the source for this historical example.

claim: The main goal of the BashTheBug citizen science project is to reduce MIC measurement error in the large dataset of 20,637 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates collected by the CRyPTIC project.
source: The main goal of the BashTheBug citizen science project, which was launched in April 2017 on the Zooniverse platform, is to reduce MIC measurement error in the large dataset of 20,637 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates collected by the Comprehensive Resistance Prediction for Tuberculosis: an International Consortium (CRyPTIC) project.
evidence: The claim is stated directly as the project's main objective.

claim: BashTheBug was launched as a project on the Zooniverse citizen science platform on 8 April 2017.
source: After a successful beta-test on 22 March 2017, BashTheBug was launched as a project on the Zooniverse citizen science platform on 8 April 2017.
evidence: The claim provides specific dates for the project launch.

claim: By the end of the first week, 2029 people had participated (of which 1,259 had usernames) classifying a total of 74,949 images.
source: By the end of the first week, 2029 people had participated (of which 1,259 had usernames) classifying a total of 74,949 images – this includes the beta-test.
evidence: The claim provides specific participation statistics from the first week.

claim: The initial set of images were completed on 11 October 2017.
source: The initial set of images were completed on 11 October 2017 and a second set was classified between 8 June 2020 and 15 November 2020 (Figure 1A) to increase the number of classifications per drug image from 11 to 17.
evidence: The claim provides specific dates and references Figure 1A for visual confirmation.

claim: A second set of images was classified between 8 June 2020 and 15 November 2020 to increase the number of classifications per drug image from 11 to 17.
source: The initial set of images were completed on 11 October 2017 and a second set was classified between 8 June 2020 and 15 November 2020 (Figure 1A) to increase the number of classifications per drug image from 11 to 17.
evidence: The claim provides specific dates and rationale, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In total, 9372 volunteers participated in classifying this dataset doing a total of 778,202 classifications.
source: In total, 9372 volunteers participated in classifying this dataset doing a total of 778,202 classifications (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim provides specific participation statistics and references a figure.

claim: On 251 of the 356 days (70%) when these data were being collected there were ten or more volunteers active on the project.
source: On 251 of the 356 days (70 %) when these data were being collected there were ten or more volunteers active on the project (Figure 1B), and on 31% of the days 50 or more volunteers were active.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about volunteer activity and references Figure 1B.

claim: Almost half of the volunteers (4299) did ten or fewer classifications and 1115 classified only a single image.
source: Almost half of the volunteers (4299) did ten or fewer classifications and 1115 classified only a single image whilst the ten volunteers who participated the most did 103,569 classifications between them which is 13.1% of the total.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about the distribution of volunteer participation.

claim: The ten volunteers who participated the most did 103,569 classifications between them which is 13.1% of the total.
source: Almost half of the volunteers (4299) did ten or fewer classifications and 1115 classified only a single image whilst the ten volunteers who participated the most did 103,569 classifications between them which is 13.1% of the total.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about the most active volunteers.

claim: The Gini-coefficient for BashTheBug is 0.85.
source: The Gini-coefficient is a useful way to measure these unequal levels of participation, and for this dataset it is 0.85 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim provides a specific statistical measure and references Figure 1C.

claim: A total of 381,964 classifications were done in the first hundred days after launch by a total of 6237 users of which 3733 were registered.
source: A total of 381,964 classifications were done in the first hundred days after launch by a total of 6237 users of which 3733 were registered and so were unique.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about the first 100 days of the project.

claim: Cox et al., 2015 measured a mean Gini coefficient across several Zooniverse projects of 0.81.
source: Cox et al., 2015 measured a mean Gini coefficient across several Zooniverse projects of 0.81, whilst a later and more comprehensive study Spiers et al., 2019 demonstrated that Zooniverse projects had Gini coefficients in the range 0.54–0.94 with a mean of 0.80.
evidence: The claim cites Cox et al., 2015 as the source for the mean Gini coefficient.

claim: Zooniverse projects had Gini coefficients in the range 0.54–0.94 with a mean of 0.80.
source: Cox et al., 2015 measured a mean Gini coefficient across several Zooniverse projects of 0.81, whilst a later and more comprehensive study Spiers et al., 2019 demonstrated that Zooniverse projects had Gini coefficients in the range 0.54–0.94 with a mean of 0.80.
evidence: The claim cites Spiers et al., 2019 as the source for the range and mean of Gini coefficients.

claim: Biomedical projects had lower Gini coefficients, with a mean Gini coefficient of 0.67.
source: They also suggested that biomedical projects had lower Gini coefficients, with a mean Gini coefficient of 0.67; however, this was only based on three projects.
evidence: The claim is stated with a caveat about the limited sample size.

claim: BashTheBug attracted more users, completed more classifications and had a higher Gini coefficient than any of the three biomedical projects studied by Spiers et al., 2019.
source: BashTheBug attracted more users, completed more classifications and had a higher Gini coefficient than any of these three biomedical projects (Spiers et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim compares BashTheBug to other biomedical projects cited in Spiers et al., 2019.

claim: Etch-a-cell, a more recent biomedical project that launched at a similar time to BashTheBug, had a Gini coefficient of 0.83.
source: A more recent biomedical project, Etch-a-cell, that launched at a similar time to BashTheBug had a Gini coefficient of 0.83 (Spiers et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Spiers et al., 2020 as the source for the Gini coefficient of Etch-a-cell.

claim: BashTheBug has a higher than average level of participation inequality, having the 17th highest Gini coefficient out of 63 Zooniverse projects surveyed.
source: BashTheBug therefore has a higher than average level of participation inequality, having the 17th highest Gini coefficient out of 63 Zooniverse projects surveyed (Spiers et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim cites Spiers et al., 2019 and provides a specific ranking.

claim: The distribution of time spent per image shows no appreciable differences when calculated as function of the incubation time with a mode of 3.5 s.
source: The distribution of time spent per image shows no appreciable differences when calculated as function of the incubation time with a mode of 3.5 s (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which is unexpected given after only 7 days of incubation there is little or no bacterial growth.
evidence: The claim provides a specific statistical measure and references figures showing the data.

claim: After 14 days incubation there are observable differences between how long the volunteers spent classifying each drug.
source: After 14 days incubation there are, however, observable differences between how long the volunteers spent classifying each drug (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim references a figure showing differences in classification time by drug.

claim: Each drug image was also measured by a laboratory scientist using a Vizion instrument as well as programmatically by some software, AMyGDA.
source: Each drug image was also measured by a laboratory scientist using a Vizion instrument as well as programmatically by some software, AMyGDA (Fowler, 2017).
evidence: The claim describes the methods used for expert measurements and cites the AMyGDA software.

claim: AMyGDA software will often classify artefacts, such as air bubbles, contamination, shadows and sediment, as bacterial growth.
source: Although the AMyGDA software is reproducible, it will often classify artefacts, such as air bubbles, contamination, shadows and sediment, as bacterial growth and is also likely to assess a well as containing no bacterial growth when the level of growth is very low.
evidence: The claim describes known limitations of the AMyGDA software.

claim: Laboratory scientists are less consistent but can recognise and ignore artefacts.
source: By contrast, laboratory scientists are less consistent but can recognise and ignore artefacts.
evidence: The claim compares the characteristics of human experts versus software.

claim: A total of 12,488 drug images were read after 14 days incubation.
source: A total of 12,488 drug images were read after 14 days incubation (Supplementary file 1); for 6205 (49.7%) of these both the laboratory scientist (Expert) and the software (AMyGDA) returned the same MIC.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about the dataset.

claim: For 6205 (49.7%) of the 12,488 drug images read after 14 days incubation, both the laboratory scientist and AMyGDA returned the same MIC.
source: A total of 12,488 drug images were read after 14 days incubation (Supplementary file 1); for 6205 (49.7%) of these both the laboratory scientist (Expert) and the software (AMyGDA) returned the same MIC.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about agreement between methods.

claim: A laboratory scientist would be reasonably expected to make an error ≤ 5% of the time.
source: Since a laboratory scientist would be reasonably expected to make an error ≤ 5% of the time, the majority of the drug images excluded are most likely due to AMyGDA incorrectly reading a drug image with only a minority being genuine errors.
evidence: The claim is stated as a reasonable expectation about expert error rates.

claim: The average level of growth in the positive controls for the Expert+AMyGDA dataset (30.4%) is similar to that observed (30.6%) for the larger Expert dataset.
source: We can show that this is not the case since not only is the average level of growth in the positive controls (as measured by AMyGDA) for the Expert+AMyGDA dataset (30.4%) similar to that observed (30.6%) for the larger Expert dataset (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), but the distributions themselves are very similar.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics and references a figure showing the distributions.

claim: The probability of the Expert+AMyGDA measurements agreeing is a function of the dilution MIC.
source: This would imply that the probability of the Expert+AMyGDA measurements agreeing is a function of the dilution MIC, which indeed is what we find (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: The agreement is highest when there is no growth in any of the drug wells.
source: The agreement is highest when there is no growth in any of the drug wells, which makes sense as that is a relatively trivial classification to make.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the data and logical reasoning.

claim: The Expert+AMyGDA dataset has a different distribution of measured MICs, including a greater proportion of drug images with a low MIC dilution (61.4% after 14 days incubation have a dilution of 1 or 2) compared to the parent Expert dataset (45.8%).
source: The net effect of this is that the Expert+AMyGDA dataset has a different distribution of measured MICs, including a greater proportion of drug images with a low MIC dilution (61.4% after 14 days incubation have a dilution of 1 or 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 4) compared to the parent Expert dataset (45.8%).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics and references a figure.

claim: There is no international standard for Mycobacterial AST.
source: Unfortunately, there is no international standard for Mycobacterial AST – the need to subject Mycobacteria to the same processes and standards as other bacteria has been argued elsewhere (Schön et al., 2020) – we shall therefore tentatively apply the international standard for aerobic bacteria (International Standards Organization, 2007) which requires the results of the proposed antibiotic susceptibility testing method to an appropriate reference method.
evidence: The claim cites Schön et al., 2020 and notes the absence of a standard.

claim: Broth microdilution using Middlebrook 7H9 media was recently selected by EUCAST as a reference method for determining M. tuberculosis MICs.
source: Neither of the measurement methods used in constructing our reference consensus dataset has been endorsed, although broth microdilution using Middlebrook 7H9 media was recently selected by EUCAST as a reference method for determining M. tuberculosis MICs (Schön et al., 2020) but only for manually-prepared 96-well plates, permitting much larger numbers of wells for each drug.
evidence: The claim cites Schön et al., 2020 as the source for EUCAST's selection.

claim: ISO 20776–2 requires a new AST method that measures MICs to be compared to the reference method using two key metrics: the exact agreement and the essential agreement.
source: This requires a new AST method that measures MICs to be compared to the reference method using two key metrics: the exact agreement and the essential agreement.
evidence: The claim describes requirements from the ISO standard.

claim: Essential agreement is defined as the MIC result obtained by the AST device that is within plus or minus doubling dilution step from the MIC value established by the reference method.
source: The former is simply the proportion of definite readings which agree, whilst the latter allows for some variability and is defined as the "MIC result obtained by the AST device that is within plus or minus doubling dilution step from the MIC value established by the reference method" (International Standards Organization, 2007).
evidence: The claim quotes the definition from the ISO standard.

claim: To meet the ISO standard any new AST method must be ≥95% reproducible and ≥90% accurate (both assessed using essential agreement) compared to the reference method.
source: To meet the standard any new AST method must be ≥95% reproducible and ≥90% accurate (both assessed using essential agreement) compared to the reference method (International Standards Organization, 2007).
evidence: The claim cites the ISO standard for the required thresholds.

claim: A single volunteer is likely to exactly agree with the Expert +AMyGDA dataset 74.6% of the time, excluding cases where either concluded the drug image could not be read.
source: Examining all 112,163 classifications made by the volunteers on the 6205 drug images taken after 14 days incubation and comparing them to the consensus of the laboratory scientist and AMyGDA shows that a single volunteer is likely to exactly agree with the Expert +AMyGDA dataset 74.6% of the time, excluding cases where either concluded the drug image could not be read (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics from the analysis.

claim: A single volunteer's essential agreement with the Expert +AMyGDA dataset rises to 86.4%.
source: This rises to 86.4% when only considering essential agreement.
evidence: The claim provides a specific statistic for essential agreement.

claim: If the consensus view is that a drug image contains no growth, a single volunteer is likely to agree 64.1% of the time.
source: The magnitude of agreement varies depending on the measured dilution: if the consensus view is that a drug image contains no growth, a single volunteer is likely to agree 64.1% of the time (Figure 2A), however this falls to 47.8% if the consensus dataset indicates that the first four wells contain growth before rising to 94.5% when the laboratory scientist decides the dilution is 8.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics and references Figure 2A.

claim: Drug images with no growth or growth in all wells are easier to read than drug images where only a subset of drug wells contain growth.
source: We hence recapitulate our earlier observation that drug images with no growth or growth in all wells are easier to read than drug images where only a subset of drug wells contain growth.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the agreement statistics.

claim: The BashTheBug volunteers are likely to return a higher dilution than the Expert +AMyGDA consensus.
source: The BashTheBug volunteers are likely to return a higher dilution than the Expert +AMyGDA consensus; this can be seen in the greater proportion of MICs with higher dilutions (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: A single volunteer is at least 5×, and often > 10×, more likely to return an MIC one greater than the reference rather than an MIC one lower than the reference.
source: For example a single volunteer is at least 5 ×, and often > 10 ×, more likely to return an MIC one greater than the reference rather than an MIC one lower than the reference (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics and references Figure 2D.

claim: An individual volunteer is less likely to agree with a single laboratory scientist with the overall level of exact agreement falling from 74.6% to 65.3%.
source: Comparing the classifications made by individual volunteers with the larger, but presumably less accurate, Expert dataset we see that an individual volunteer is less likely to agree with a single laboratory scientist with the overall level of exact agreement falling from 74.6% to 65.3% (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics comparing agreement with different reference datasets.

claim: Consensus measurements formed by taking the mode are more likely to exactly agree with one another (89.2 ± 0.1%) than the median (86.9 ± 0.1%) or mean (74.3 ± 0.1%).
source: Considering only those drug images taken after 14 days incubation (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1e), they are more likely to exactly agree with one another when the mode was applied (89.2 ± 0.1%) than the median (86.9 ± 0.1%) or mean (74.3 ± 0.1%).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics with standard errors and references figures.

claim: For essential agreement in reproducibility, the mean performs best (97.2 ± 0.1%), followed by the median (94.2 ± 0.1%) and mode (94.1 ± 0.1%).
source: For the essential agreement, we find that the mean now performs best (97.2 ± 0.1%), followed by the median (94.2 ± 0.1%) and mode (94.1 ± 0.1%).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics with standard errors.

claim: The reproducibility for MICs measured by two laboratory scientists, as quantified by essential agreement, was previously shown to be 97.9%.
source: As one might expect, the reproducibility for MICs measured by two laboratory scientists, as quantified by essential agreement, was previously shown to be slightly higher, at 97.9 % (Rancoita et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Rancoita et al., 2018 for the expert reproducibility statistic.

claim: Only calculating the mean of 17 classifications achieves an essential agreement ≥95% for reproducibility.
source: Hence only the mean exceeds the threshold for reproducibility (International Standards Organization, 2007) when 17 classifications are used to build a consensus.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to the ISO standard threshold.

claim: The mode exactly agrees with the Expert+AMyGDA reference 80.9 ± 0.1% of the time, followed by the median (78.1 ± 0.1%) and then mean (68.4 ± 0.1%).
source: The mode exactly agrees with the reference 80.9 ± 0.1% of the time, followed by the median (78.1 ± 0.1%) and then mean (68.4 ± 0.1%).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics with standard errors for accuracy.

claim: The mean has the lowest level of essential agreement with the Expert+AMyGDA readings (88.5 ± 0.1%), with the median (90.2 ± 0.1%) and mode (91.0 ± 0.1%) both exceeding the 90% accuracy threshold.
source: The mean, despite performing best for reproducibility, has the lowest level of essential agreement (as well as exact agreement) with the Expert+AMyGDA readings (88.5 ± 0.1%), with the median (90.2 ± 0.1%) and mode (91.0 ± 0.1%) both exceeding the 90% accuracy threshold (International Standards Organization, 2007).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics and compares them to the ISO standard threshold.

claim: The consensus dilution of the classifications made by the volunteers is much more likely to be higher than the Expert+AMyGDA measurement than lower.
source: The heatmaps show how the consensus dilution of the classifications made by the volunteers is much more likely to be higher than the Expert+AMyGDA measurement than lower (Figure 3D), regardless of the consensus method, indicating perhaps that volunteers are more likely than laboratory scientists to classify any dark regions in a well as bacterial growth, or that laboratory scientists are more willing to discount some features as artefacts for example air bubbles or sediment.
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in heatmaps and includes speculation about the cause.

claim: The median and mode have very similar reproducibilities and accuracy and perform equally well.
source: The median and mode have very similar reproducibilities and accuracy and we conclude they perform equally well.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the statistical comparisons.

claim: Bi-modal classification distributions are rare and the median is often identical to the mode.
source: We can infer from this that bi-modal classification distributions are rare and that the median is often identical to the mode.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the similarity of median and mode performance.

claim: Accuracy is less sensitive than reproducibility to reducing the number of classifications used to build the consensus.
source: Accuracy is hence less sensitive than reproducibility to reducing the number of classifications used to build the consensus and, depending on the consensus method used, the number of classifications can be reduced whilst still maintaining acceptable levels of accuracy.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the analysis of how performance changes with n.

claim: The amount of growth in the positive control wells has little effect on either the reproducibility or accuracy, regardless of the consensus method and number of classifications employed.
source: One might expect that drug images with poor growth would be more challenging to classify, however, segmenting by low, medium and high growth shows the amount of growth in the positive control wells has little effect on either the reproducibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) or accuracy (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), regardless of the consensus method and number of classifications employed.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of data segmented by growth level and references figures.

claim: A simple dynamic approach to retiring images would minimise the work done by the volunteers / allow more images to be classified.
source: We therefore conclude that even a simple dynamic approach to retiring images would minimise the work done by the volunteers / allow more images to be classified.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the analysis of dynamic retirement strategies.

claim: The reproducibility of each drug, as measured by the exact and essential agreements, varies between 79.6–91.4% and 90.8–97.0%, respectively.
source: The reproducibility of each drug, as measured by the exact and essential agreements, varies between 79.6–91.4% and 90.8–97.0%, respectively (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim provides specific ranges and references Figure 5A.

claim: Intra- and inter-laboratory reproducibility when the drugs were read by a scientist using a Vizion instrument varied between 93.4-99.3% and 87.1-99.1% (as measured by essential agreement, excl. PAS), respectively.
source: This is consistent with an earlier study which found that intra- and inter-laboratory reproducibility when the drugs were read by a scientist using a Vizion instrument varied between 93.4-99.3 % and 87.1-99.1 % (as measured by essential agreement, excl. PAS), respectively (Rancoita et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Rancoita et al., 2018 for comparison data.

claim: Five out of the 13 drugs meet or exceed the 95% reproducibility threshold whilst the plate as a whole does not.
source: Applying the same threshold to each drug we find that five out of the 13 drugs meet or exceed the threshold whilst the plate as a whole does not.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to the ISO standard threshold.

claim: The accuracy of each drug varies between 48.4–88.9% and 82.8–94.7% when assessed using the exact and essential agreement, respectively.
source: The accuracy of each drug varies more widely: between 48.4–88.9% and 82.8–94.7% when assessed using the exact and essential agreement, respectively.
evidence: The claim provides specific ranges for accuracy by drug.

claim: Only six out of 13 drugs surpassed the 90% accuracy threshold.
source: Hence whilst the accuracy of the plate as a whole was 90.2 ± 0.1%, just exceeding the 90% threshold, only six out of 13 drugs surpassed the same threshold.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to the ISO standard threshold.

claim: The variation in reproducibility and accuracy between anti-tuberculars is due to a number of factors, including the number and concentration range of the wells on the plate design, the mechanisms of both action and resistance, the prevalence of resistance and the degradation rate after lyophilisation.
source: The variation in reproducibility and accuracy between anti-tuberculars, as well as between the exact and essential agreement for a single compound, is due to a number of factors, not limited to the number and concentration range of the wells on the plate design, the mechanisms of both action and resistance, the prevalence of resistance and the degradation rate after lyophilisation, both during storage and after inoculation.
evidence: The claim lists multiple factors that could affect performance.

claim: Kanamycin passes the reproducibility and accuracy thresholds likely due to there being relatively few (five) drug wells on the UKMYC5 plate.
source: For example, kanamycin passes the reproducibility and accuracy thresholds we have adopted and this is likely due to there being relatively few (five) drug wells on the UKMYC5 plate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and the mechanism of resistance being such a substantial proportion of samples either do not grow in any well, or grow in all the drug wells, making measurement more straightforward.
evidence: The claim provides a specific example and speculates about the reasons.

claim: From the striking differences in exact and essential accuracies of reading ethambutol, moxifloxacin and linezolid, the Mycobacterial growth diminishes more gradually with increasing concentration for these drugs.
source: From the striking differences in exact and essential accuracies of reading ethambutol, moxifloxacin and linezolid we hypothesise the Mycobacterial growth diminishes more gradually with increasing concentration for these drugs, rather than coming to an abrupt end, as it does for other compounds.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on observed differences in accuracy metrics.

claim: A crowd of volunteers can reproducibly and accurately measure the growth of a bacterial pathogen on a 96-well broth microdilution plate.
source: A crowd of volunteers can reproducibly and accurately measure the growth of a bacterial pathogen on a 96-well broth microdilution plate, thereby demonstrating the potential for clinical microbiology to embrace and combine contrasting measurement methods.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The reproducibility of the median and mode, as measured by the essential agreement, is 94.2% and 94.1%, respectively.
source: Forming a consensus by applying the mode or median to 17 independent classifications performs better overall than the mean, and the reproducibility of both these methods, as measured by the essential agreement, is 94.2% and 94.1%, respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics and references a figure.

claim: The volunteers do not pass the 95% reproducibility threshold set by ISO for aerobic bacteria.
source: This is below than the 95% threshold set by ISO for aerobic bacteria and therefore the volunteers do not pass this standard.
evidence: The claim compares the results to the ISO standard.

claim: The accuracy of the crowd, as measured by the essential agreement, is 90.2% and 91.0% when the median and mode, respectively, are applied.
source: The accuracy of the crowd, as measured by the essential agreement, is 90.2% and 91.0% when the median and mode, respectively, are applied to produce a consensus measurement – these values are above the required 90% threshold (International Standards Organization, 2007), and therefore the volunteers are sufficiently accurate (but not quite reproducible enough) to be classified as an antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) device.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics and compares them to the ISO standard.

claim: The volunteers are sufficiently accurate (but not quite reproducible enough) to be classified as an antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) device.
source: The accuracy of the crowd, as measured by the essential agreement, is 90.2% and 91.0% when the median and mode, respectively, are applied to produce a consensus measurement – these values are above the required 90% threshold (International Standards Organization, 2007), and therefore the volunteers are sufficiently accurate (but not quite reproducible enough) to be classified as an antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) device.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison to ISO standards.

claim: The consensus readings made by the crowd of volunteers have been successfully used within the CRyPTIC project to reduce the measurement error in the dataset of 268,281 minimum inhibitory concentrations.
source: The BashTheBug project has therefore been successful in its primary aim, i.e. the consensus readings made by the crowd of volunteers have been successfully used within the CRyPTIC project to reduce the measurement error in the dataset of 268,281 (13 drugs × 20,637 samples) minimum inhibitory concentrations.
evidence: The claim states the successful achievement of the project's primary aim.

claim: CRyPTIC has significantly contributed to the first resistance catalogue published by the World Health Organization.
source: CRyPTIC has already significantly contributed to the first resistance catalogue published by the World Health Organization (Walker et al., 2022), carried out the largest genome-wide association study of M. tuberculosis (The CRyPTIC Consortium, 2021) and assessed the magnitude of MIC-shifts for the most common mutations that confer resistance (The CRyPTIC Consortium, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Walker et al., 2022 for the WHO resistance catalogue contribution.

claim: CRyPTIC carried out the largest genome-wide association study of M. tuberculosis.
source: CRyPTIC has already significantly contributed to the first resistance catalogue published by the World Health Organization (Walker et al., 2022), carried out the largest genome-wide association study of M. tuberculosis (The CRyPTIC Consortium, 2021) and assessed the magnitude of MIC-shifts for the most common mutations that confer resistance (The CRyPTIC Consortium, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites The CRyPTIC Consortium, 2021 for the GWAS study.

claim: Genetics-based AST is already faster and cheaper than the culture-based alternatives for tuberculosis.
source: The intention is to accelerate the shift from culture-based to genetics-based AST, which is already faster and cheaper than the culture-based alternatives for tuberculosis (Pankhurst et al., 2016) and this is well underway (Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Pankhurst et al., 2016 for the comparison of genetics-based vs culture-based AST.

claim: The volunteers are fast, taking on average 3.5 s per drug image.
source: The volunteers are fast, taking on average 3.5 s per drug image, and therefore a single plate requires slightly less than 13 min of volunteer time to read if 17 classifications are amassed for each drug.
evidence: The claim provides specific timing statistics.

claim: A single plate requires slightly less than 13 min of volunteer time to read if 17 classifications are amassed for each drug.
source: The volunteers are fast, taking on average 3.5 s per drug image, and therefore a single plate requires slightly less than 13 min of volunteer time to read if 17 classifications are amassed for each drug.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the average time per image.

claim: Ten volunteers did, on average, over 10,000 classifications each.
source: The level of participation by the volunteers was very unequal with a small cadre of volunteers doing very large numbers with ten volunteers doing, on average, over 10,000 classifications each which is more than many of the laboratory scientists who are considered the experts!
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about the most active volunteers.

claim: The consensus dilution arrived at by the volunteers tends to be higher than measurements taken by laboratory scientists, indicating a bias to overcall.
source: Compared to the measurements taken by the laboratory scientists, the consensus dilution arrived at by the volunteers tends to be higher, indicating a bias to overcall (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which is supported by anecdotal observations of people classifying drug images at public engagement events where they often choose a higher dilution 'to be on the safe side'.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis and anecdotal observations.

claim: As volunteers do more classifications they become more experienced and the magnitude of the bias reduces but does not disappear.
source: As volunteers do more classifications they become more experienced and, on the whole, the magnitude of the bias reduces but does not disappear (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of volunteer performance over time and references a figure.

claim: The AMyGDA computer software is more likely to undercall compared to the expert.
source: By contrast, the AMyGDA computer software has been noted to have the opposite bias – that is is more likely to undercall compared to the expert (Fowler et al., 2018c).
evidence: The claim cites Fowler et al., 2018c for the observation about AMyGDA bias.

claim: The reproducibility and accuracy of any method used to read a 96-well microtitre plate depends on a range of factors from the prevalence of drug-resistant samples in the dataset to which drugs are included in the plate design and the number and concentrations of their allotted wells.
source: The reproducibility and accuracy of any method used to read a 96-well microtitre plate, whether that is laboratory scientists using a Thermo Fisher Vizion instrument or citizen scientists visually examining drug images, depends on a range of factors from the prevalence of drug-resistant samples in the dataset to which drugs are included in the plate design and the number and concentrations of their allotted wells.
evidence: The claim lists multiple factors affecting performance.

claim: Both the Expert and either the AMyGDA or BashTheBug measurements are more likely to agree with one another at low dilutions where there is little or no M. tuberculosis growth in the drug wells.
source: For the UKMYC5 plate design, both the Expert and either the AMyGDA or BashTheBug measurements are more likely to agree with one another at low dilutions where there is little or no M. tuberculosis growth in the drug wells (Supplementary file 1d, i), hence reducing the number of resistant samples would artificially 'improve' performance yet the standards do not specify the degree of resistance in any test dataset (International Standards Organization, 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis and notes a limitation of the standards.

claim: The dataset used was based on 19 external quality assessment strains.
source: The dataset used here was based on 19 external quality assessment strains and therefore whilst it included some degree of resistance for all 13 drugs, there was only a single strain resistant to clofazimine, bedaquiline or delamanid and no strain was resistant to linezolid (Rancoita et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim describes the composition of the dataset and cites the source.

claim: For isoniazid and rifampicin, eight and seven of the 19 EQA strains, respectively were resistant.
source: For isoniazid and rifampicin, eight and seven of the 19 EQA strains, respectively were resistant and hence the prevalence of resistance for these drugs is much greater than would be expected to be encountered in most countries.
evidence: The claim provides specific statistics about resistance prevalence in the dataset.

claim: The resulting dataset of classifications is ideally suited to train machine-learning models.
source: Although the primary aim of this study was to assess whether the measurements produced by a crowd of volunteers are sufficiently reproducible and accurate to help reduce the measurement error in datasets containing large numbers of microtitre plates (as is being collected by the CRyPTIC project and others) the resulting dataset of classifications is ideally suited to train machine-learning models.
evidence: The claim identifies a secondary use for the dataset.

claim: Training machine-learning models is increasingly recognised as an important use of citizen science.
source: This is increasingly recognised as an important use of citizen science (Trouille et al., 2019) and one could envisage training a light-weight machine-learning algorithm able to run on a mobile device which, by taking a photograph of a 96-well plate, could automatically read the minimum inhibitory concentrations.
evidence: The claim cites Trouille et al., 2019 for the recognition of this use of citizen science.
